name: Vehicle General Safety Regulation
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: applies to all new vehicles since July 2024 and the first Commission evaluation is due in July 2027; studies of the same systems fitted voluntarily before the mandate measure their effect on crashes
summary: The mandatory safety systems apply to new vehicle types since July 2022 and to all new vehicles since July 2024; the Commission must report on their effect, including real-world performance of intelligent speed assistance, by 7 July 2027. Studies of the same systems fitted voluntarily before the mandate found that automatic emergency braking cut rear-end crashes by 38% and lane-keeping systems cut the crashes they target by 53%, while emergency braking for pedestrians showed no clear effect, none at all in darkness.

literature.citation: European Commission (2018), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal on type-approval requirements for motor vehicles as regards their general safety, SWD(2018) 190 (executive summary SWD(2018) 191)
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal on type-approval requirements for motor vehicles as regards their general safety
literature.headline: Mandatory advanced safety systems expected to reduce road deaths and serious injuries; costs passed on in vehicle prices
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected the new mandatory safety systems to save lives on EU roads.

literature.citation: Fildes, B.; Keall, M.; Bos, N.; Lie, A.; Page, Y.; Pastor, C.; Pennisi, L.; Rizzi, M.; Thomas, P.; Tingvall, C. (2015), Effectiveness of low speed autonomous emergency braking in real-world rear-end crashes, Accident Analysis & Prevention 81:24-29
literature.authors: Fildes, B.; Keall, M.; Bos, N.; Lie, A.; Page, Y.; Pastor, C.; Pennisi, L.; Rizzi, M.; Thomas, P.; Tingvall, C.
literature.title: Effectiveness of low speed autonomous emergency braking in real-world rear-end crashes
literature.method: meta-analysis of pooled police/insurance crash data from several countries, induced-exposure (MUND) approach
literature.headline: Vehicles fitted with low-speed AEB had a 38% overall reduction in rear-end crashes vs comparable vehicles, with no statistical difference between urban (<=60 km/h) and rural speed zones.
literature.summary_plain: Automatic emergency braking, one of the systems the GSR made mandatory, cut rear-end crashes by over a third in real-world data.
literature.quality: quasi-experimental (induced exposure); voluntary-fitment era, not an evaluation of the mandate itself
literature.interested_party: collaboration includes vehicle-industry researchers (e.g. Renault) and Euro NCAP-linked bodies

literature.citation: Kullgren, A.; Amin, K.; Tingvall, C. (2023), Effects on crash risk of automatic emergency braking systems for pedestrians and bicyclists, Traffic Injury Prevention 24(sup1):S111-S115
literature.authors: Kullgren, A.; Amin, K.; Tingvall, C.
literature.title: Effects on crash risk of automatic emergency braking systems for pedestrians and bicyclists
literature.method: induced-exposure odds ratios on Swedish STRADA police and hospital crash data, model years 2015-2020
literature.headline: AEB with cyclist detection reduced cyclist crash risk by 21% (+/-17%). AEB with pedestrian detection gave a non-significant 8% (+/-15%) reduction, and neither showed any reduction in darkness.
literature.summary_plain: Emergency braking that detects cyclists helps, but the pedestrian version showed no clear effect and none at night, which matters because the GSR mandates pedestrian/cyclist AEB.

literature.citation: Sternlund, S.; Strandroth, J.; Rizzi, M.; Lie, A.; Tingvall, C. (2017), The effectiveness of lane departure warning systems - A reduction in real-world passenger car injury crashes, Traffic Injury Prevention 18(2):225-229
literature.authors: Sternlund, S.; Strandroth, J.; Rizzi, M.; Lie, A.; Tingvall, C.
literature.title: The effectiveness of lane departure warning systems - A reduction in real-world passenger car injury crashes
literature.method: induced-exposure comparison of Volvo cars with and without LDW/LKA, Swedish STRADA data (1,853 injury crashes)
literature.headline: LDW/LKA reduced head-on and single-vehicle injury crashes by 53% (lower 95% CI limit 11%) on 70-120 km/h roads with dry or wet surfaces, and by 30% (lower limit 6%) across all such crashes.
literature.summary_plain: Lane-keeping and lane-departure warning systems, now mandated by the GSR, roughly halved the run-off-road and head-on crashes they target in Swedish data.
literature.quality: quasi-experimental; small treated sample (146 LDW, 11 LKA cars); single brand
literature.interested_party: co-authors from Swedish Transport Administration (road-safety authority)

literature.citation: Lai, F.; Carsten, O.; Tate, F. (2012), How much benefit does Intelligent Speed Adaptation deliver: An analysis of its potential contribution to safety and environment, Accident Analysis & Prevention 48:63-72
literature.authors: Lai, F.; Carsten, O.; Tate, F.
literature.title: How much benefit does Intelligent Speed Adaptation deliver: An analysis of its potential contribution to safety and environment
literature.method: field-trial driver-behaviour data (UK ISA project) extrapolated to crash and CO2 impacts; cost-benefit appraisal
literature.headline: ISA was predicted to save up to 33% of crashes on urban roads and 30% of fatal and 25% of serious crashes over 60 years, with benefit-cost ratios of 3.4-7.4.
literature.summary_plain: UK trials suggested speed-limiting assistance could prevent many crashes, but this is a prediction, not a measured effect of the EU mandate.
literature.quality: ex-ante projection from field trials; not an evaluation of the mandate

literature.citation: Pissarra da Costa, A.; Innamaa, S.; Malin, F. (2025), Safety impact of advanced driver assistance systems in Europe in 2030, Journal of Safety Research 95:290-300
literature.authors: Pissarra da Costa, A.; Innamaa, S.; Malin, F.
literature.title: Safety impact of advanced driver assistance systems in Europe in 2030
literature.method: effect sizes from literature combined with fleet-penetration and target-crash projections for EU-27
literature.outcomes: projected injury crash reduction from GSR-mandated ADAS by 2030
literature.headline: Mandated AEB, LKA, advisory ISA and reversing cameras together were projected to cut injury car crashes in the EU-27 by 6% in 2030 vs a 2019 fitment baseline. AEB accounts for 5%, ISA 1%, and LKA and reverse cameras 0.2% each.
literature.summary_plain: By 2030 the GSR's mandatory driver-assist systems are expected to cut injury crashes by about 6%, helpful but far short of the EU's goal of halving casualties.

literature.citation: Carboni, A.; Deflorio, F.P.; Cossu, F.; Scotto, F.C. (2025), Observing user perception and usage of ADAS from a survey in Italy, Transportation Research Procedia 90:647-654
literature.authors: Carboni, A.; Deflorio, F.P.; Cossu, F.; Scotto, F.C.
literature.title: Observing user perception and usage of ADAS from a survey in Italy
literature.outcomes: knowledge, use and deactivation of ADAS including ISA
literature.headline: In 9,078 responses, ISA was the least known of the systems surveyed. The main reason drivers gave for deactivating ADAS was the 'desire to be in full control of the car'; the GSR allows drivers to switch the systems off.
literature.summary_plain: Many Italian drivers do not know about speed assistance, and those who switch systems off say they want full control, which could blunt the GSR's benefits.
